final_explanation: Justin's profile emerges from 21 reads spanning an IELTS speaking-test interview conducted in his second language (French L1). Openness (medium): genuine enthusiasm for travel and novelty surfaces beyond prompt-compliance in M8 ('Oh absolutely, I love traveling to new countries,' fast-paced, specific 'almost every place' claim) and M9 (energy lift on 'meet new people, see new faces'); sensory-experiential preference in M4 (values hearing a voice, 'getting a feeling'); breadth of cultural interest in M10/M20 (Prehistoric Museum, art galleries) and M13/M14 (WWII history, shipwrecks, churches). However, much of this is elicited by structured questions, and his grounded, practical descriptions (farmers in M15, industrialization in M14) temper the picture to medium rather than high. Conscientiousness (medium): recurring organizational instincts—bookend repetition in M15, systematic contrast framework in M12, definitive close in M16, clean single-sentence in M3—go beyond the minimum the setting demands. Yet trailing-offs (M5 'I think I'd probably say' incomplete; M14 ends mid-phrase at clip edge, which per protocol is not behavior) and frequent fillers signal imperfect planning. The balance of structure-with-gaps supports medium. Extraversion (medium): animated delivery on self-selected topics—broad open-palm gestures and rising pitch in M4, immediate high-energy response in M8, smile/laugh in M7, eyebrow-raise and outward hand gesture in M9/M10/M20—contrasts with contained, still posture in M3, M5, M16. The animation is topic-contingent rather than uniformly outgoing; he engages expressively when passionate but defaults to economy on administrative/factual prompts. The interview setting and L2 constrain baseline expressiveness, so the observed peaks represent genuine choice, placing him at medium. Agreeableness (high): consistent cooperative stance across M2 (prompt ID compliance, silent composed wait), M17/M19/M21 (flat 'Sure' acceptances of examiner framing), M12 (warm affirmation 'Oh yeah, children absolutely' before hedging), M7 (complaint delivered with self-amused laughter, not hostility), M4/M5 (opinions softened with 'in my opinion,' 'I really think,' 'probably'). The hedging, smiling, and affirm-before-qualify pattern exceeds what mere compliance requires; no dismissiveness, competitiveness, or rudeness appears in any read. Setting demands cooperation, but the *style*—warm, self-effacing, non-confrontational even when expressing dislike—supports high. Neuroticism (low): relaxed facial expression and steady gaze in M1; composed stillness during silent interval in M2; even-paced, non-anxious delivery in M3, M13; mild irritation in M7 immediately defused by laughter and 'I don't know' conversational tag; matter-of-fack acknowledgment of time/money constraints in M9 without dwelling. Fillers (um, uh, you know) recur but M1 explicitly characterizes them as pacing markers, not retrieval distress, and L2 speech naturally includes them. No sustained anxiety, fidgeting, emotional volatility, or distress is observed. Clip-edge truncations (M5, M14) are excluded per protocol. Low is supported by positive composure evidence rather than mere absence of behavior.

contextual.context: Travel/novelty prompt (M8, M9): examiner asks 'Do you enjoy traveling to different places?'
contextual.expression: Immediate, fast-paced 'Oh absolutely, I love traveling to new countries' with specific superlative claim ('almost every place'); energy lift, eyebrow raise, outward hand gesture on 'meet new people, see new faces' (M9). Goes beyond minimum answer length; selects sensory-social framing of travel value.

contextual.context: Communication-modality preference (M4, M5): examiner asks about phone vs email.
contextual.expression: Values auditory-emotional channel ('hear their voice…get a feeling for how they're feeling'); broad open-palm gestures and rising pitch on 'definitely,' 'voice,' 'feeling' (M4). Contrast: email description is slower, flatter, with dismissive lateral wave (M4) and trailing incomplete thought (M5). Shows openness to experiential richness in interaction.

contextual.context: Structured contrast task (M12): discussing children vs teenagers in hometown.
contextual.expression: Builds parallel oppositional framework: positive reasons for children (open fields, parks) then specific missing facilities for teenagers (movie theaters, gyms, cafes). Vocal pace slows and hand activity shifts from clasped stillness to finger-tapping during the hedged teenager portion ('I'd probably say not so much'), then returns to firm affirmation. Organizational instinct visible in the two-part architecture.

contextual.context: Descriptive enumeration (M15): talking about local farmers.
contextual.expression: Bookend repetition: 'a lot of them are farmers' opens and closes the segment, with concrete detail (vegetables, potatoes, farm stands, selling produce) nested between. Two 'um' fillers do not trigger restart or retraction; sentence structure continues forward. Summarizing closure technique exceeds minimum requirement of the prompt.

contextual.context: Speakerphone irritation anecdote (M6, M7): describing hearing others on trains.
contextual.expression: Firm evaluative statement 'It's the most annoying thing ever' delivered with steady forward gaze (M7), immediately followed by broad smile/laugh and self-amused repetition 'I'll I'll tell you that.' Right hand lifts in loose outward gesture illustrating sound spread. Complaint is expressed with energy and humor rather than suppressed. Contrast with M6's calmer scene-setting (hands resting, steady pace) shows the peak is topic-triggered.

contextual.context: Administrative/factual prompts (M2, M3): ID retrieval and student-status question.
contextual.expression: Single-word 'Yeah' for ID (M2), silent composed wait with clasped hands; one-sentence degree description with no fillers, no trailing elaboration, even pace, still torso (M3). Markedly more contained than the travel or communication segments. Economy here reflects the factual nature of the prompt rather than a global withdrawal; the contrast with M8/M9 animation shows extraversion is topic-contingent.

contextual.context: Complaint about speakerphone behavior (M7): evaluating a third party's action.
contextual.expression: 'Most annoying thing ever' is softened by immediate laughter, self-amused repetition, and a trailing 'I don't know' conversational tag with lowered hands and relaxed brow. The negative evaluation is directed at a behavior, not a person, and is wrapped in humor. No hostility, raised volume, or pointed accusation observed. Demonstrates agreeable processing of irritation.

contextual.context: Opinion hedging on communication preference (M4, M5) and age-group evaluation (M12).
contextual.expression: Frames preference as 'in my opinion' (M4); uses 'I really think,' 'I'd probably say' (M5, M12). Affirms children warmly ('Oh yeah, children absolutely') before qualifying teenagers ('I'd probably say not so much'). Consistent softening of assertions and affirm-before-qualify pattern across multiple topics exceeds the minimum politeness the interview protocol requires.

contextual.context: Silent waiting interval during ID review (M2) and post-answer pauses (M3, M18).
contextual.expression: Hands clasped on table, gaze forward or slightly downward, no filler words, throat-clearing, fidgeting, or vocalizations during 3-second silence (M2). After M3's answer, holds still forward gaze awaiting next prompt with no nervous movement (M18 confirms no posture change). Composed stillness in a potentially awkward L2 silence indicates low anxiety reactivity.

contextual.context: Constraint acknowledgment (M9): discussing limits on travel (time and money).
contextual.expression: Slower pace and fillers ('um,' 'you know') while stating 'I don't have as much time and money…as I feel like I would need.' Delivery is matter-of-fact, not distressed; immediately pivots with energy lift to 'but I love it. I get to meet new people.' The limitation is acknowledged without dwelling, spiraling, or visible frustration. Emotional regulation within the response supports low N.

coarse_summaries.summary: The video captures Part 1 of an IELTS speaking test conducted by examiner Mark Reed with candidate Justin Hegarty. The examiner introduces the test, collects identification, and then asks Justin about his origin and occupation. Justin identifies himself as being from Dunkirk, a small town in France on the English Channel, and states he is a student pursuing a bachelor's of science in computers. Throughout, Justin speaks in a measured, somewhat hesitant manner, using fillers like 'uh' and 'yeah,' while maintaining a seated posture with hands clasped on the table. The examiner guides the conversation with clear, formal prompts and smooth transitions between topics. A notable stretch of silence occurs during the identification check around the 20–28 second mark.

The interviewee discusses his communication habits and preferences over roughly 60 seconds. He explains that he primarily calls friends on his mobile phone, resorting to texting only when a call is impractical. When asked to compare phone and email, he strongly favors phone, citing the ability to hear the other person's voice and gauge their emotional state, while describing email as impersonal and slow due to back-and-forth exchanges. Prompted for a reason, he attributes the difference to the inability to see the other person's face. Finally, when asked about dislikes regarding mobile phones, he confirms there are several and begins describing the experience of overhearing strangers' phone conversations while riding a train. Throughout, he uses frequent hand gestures, filler words ('um,' 'you know'), and occasional self-corrections, maintaining a conversational, somewhat informal register.

The interviewee first complains about people using speakerphone in public, delivering the point with mild exasperation, self-corrections ('I'll I'll tell you that'), and trailing fillers ('I don't know'). The examiner then pivots to traveling, and the interviewee's energy shifts markedly: he responds with an emphatic 'Oh absolutely,' rapidly claims to have visited nearly every spot on a UK map, and gestures as though pointing at locations. When explaining why he travels less than he'd like, his pace slows and he inserts 'um' and 'you know' while citing time and money constraints, then brightens again describing meeting new people and seeing new faces. Finally, prompted to name specific UK places, he begins with a drawn-out 'Uh,' lists London, Birmingham, and Manchester, and singles out London Bridge and the Prehistoric Museum as favorites, speaking more deliberately as he retrieves the names.

In this segment (3:00–4:00), the examiner wraps up a topic about local attractions (art galleries) and pivots to discussing Justin's hometown in France. Justin confirms his hometown suits children well due to open fields and parks, but notes fewer facilities (movie theaters, gyms, cafés) for teenagers. When asked whether the town has changed over the years, he pauses thoughtfully, then describes Dunkirk as a very historic town, especially after World War II, mentioning ruins still visible today—old churches and shipwrecks standing. Throughout, Justin uses fillers ('um,' 'uh'), repeats affirmations ('Oh yeah, absolutely'), and gestures with his hands while explaining. The examiner remains seated, reviewing papers, occasionally nodding or interjecting brief prompts ('And why?'). The exchange is conversational, with Justin speaking at moderate pace and the examiner maintaining a calm, procedural tone.

In this ~29-second segment, the interviewee (a young man in a grey sweatshirt) finishes describing his hometown's shift toward industrialization—modern houses, more factories—using the filler "you know" and a qualifying phrase ("I would say that it's definitely…"). The examiner (an older man with glasses) then asks what jobs people do there. The interviewee answers that many are farmers who grow vegetables and potatoes over the summer, sell produce at farm stands, and repeats "a lot of them are farmers" as both opener and closer. His delivery includes several "um" and "you know" fillers, modest hand gestures when describing the farm stands, and a generally steady seated posture with hands resting or clasped on the desk. The examiner closes with "Let's see. Now…" signaling a transition to the next part of the speaking test.

Justin Hegarthy participates in a Part 1 speaking-test interview covering personal background, communication habits, travel, and his hometown of Dunkirk, France. He states he studies a Bachelor of Science in Computers, prefers phone calls over emails because he values hearing a voice and gauging mood, and finds speakerphone use on trains intensely irritating. He expresses strong enthusiasm for travel—claiming near-total UK coverage—while noting time and money as practical limits. On Dunkirk, he distinguishes between suitability for children (open fields, parks) and teenagers (few cinemas, gyms, cafés), recalls WWII-era ruins alongside present-day industrialization, and describes local farming and farm-stand commerce. His delivery oscillates between rapid, filler-laden elaboration ('um,' 'you know,' 'like,' 'things like that') and terse single-sentence replies (name, student status). He repeats openings ('I I really think,' 'I'll I'll tell you'), hedges with qualifiers ('I'd probably say,' 'I would say that'), and sometimes trails off ('I don't know'). Longer answers feature concrete scenarios and spatial imagery; shorter ones land and stop. The examiner's prompts and page-turns punctuate topic shifts.

novelty_filtered.goal: Confirm whether the examiner's 'Hmm, excellent' begins within this window and whether Justin's hand configuration is still in the open-palm explanatory phase or has already started to close, to establish the exact overlap between the interviewee's turn-end and the examiner's back-channel.

observations.content:
Justin begins his response with the filler 'Uh, yeah' and states, 'so I'm from a very small famous town called Dunkirk.' He pauses briefly with another 'Uh' before continuing, 'it's in France and it's on the English channel.' The use of these fillers appears to serve as natural pacing markers between clauses rather than indicating significant word-retrieval difficulty, as the delivery remains fluid.
Visually, Justin keeps his hands resting on the papers on the desk in front of him throughout the description. His facial expression is relaxed and engaged, with his gaze shifting slightly but generally maintaining forward orientation, consistent with someone comfortably sharing factual information.

The examiner verbally requests Justin's identification ('Okay Justin, can I see your identification please?') between approximately 0 and 4 seconds.
Justin responds with a single word 'Yeah' around 4–5 seconds, then reaches down and retrieves an ID card from his person between 5 and 7 seconds.
Justin extends the ID card toward the examiner around 7–8 seconds; the examiner takes it with his right hand while continuing to hold papers in his left.
From roughly 8 to 11 seconds, a silent interval occurs: no speech is audible from either participant.
During this silent interval, Justin remains seated with hands clasped on the table surface, gaze directed forward or slightly downward toward the examiner; no filler words, throat-clearing, or other vocalizations are heard.
During the same silent interval, the examiner holds the ID card up in his right hand at chest level while his left hand manipulates a stack of papers; his head tilts down toward the documents and he makes small page-adjusting movements.
No conversational vocalization (humming, 'mm-hm', or verbal acknowledgment) is produced by the examiner during the review pause; the gap is filled only by the physical handling of the card and papers.

The examiner (visible in frames 0–3: older man, glasses, light-blue button-down shirt, reading from a stack of papers) delivers the prompt 'That's interesting. Now, do you work or are you a student?' in a measured, note-reading cadence. His eyes remain on the page; he does not look up at Justin during the question.
Justin (visible in frames 4–6: young man, curly hair, grey crew-neck sweatshirt, seated across the desk) answers in a single compound sentence: 'Yeah, I study here. I'm a student for the bachelor's of science in computers.' No fillers ('uh,' 'um') precede or interrupt the clause, unlike the hometown reply catalogued in M1 where two 'Uh' markers segmented the description.
The response is markedly shorter than the hometown answer: one sentence naming the degree programme versus M1's multi-clause geographic sketch. Justin's vocal delivery is even-paced and falls to silence immediately after 'computers,' with no trailing elaboration or self-correction.
Visually during frames 4–6, Justin's torso stays largely still, shoulders squared toward the examiner. His gaze is directed forward (toward the examiner's side of the desk) rather than down at his own papers, and his hands are not visible in frame, suggesting they rest low or on his lap. Facial expression is neutral-to-slightly-engaged, mouth moving only for the spoken words.
After the sentence ends (~frame 6 / ≈6 s), Justin closes his mouth and holds his forward gaze, appearing to await the next prompt. No nod, hand gesture, or additional verbal tag follows; the clip ends in this waiting posture.
Relative to M1, the shift is toward economy: the hometown answer used pacing fillers and a two-part structure (town name → location), whereas this reply compresses status and programme into one breath-group. Posture in both segments is seated and forward-facing, but the hometown segment showed slight gaze drift noted in M1, while here the gaze is steadier and more fixed on the interlocutor.

The interviewee (a young man with curly hair in a grey sweatshirt, seated at a desk in an office with stacked papers and a filing cabinet behind him) states his preference for phone over email communication. He self-reports: 'definitely phone… I prefer talking to them because I can hear their voice and kind of get like a feeling for how they're feeling. Just communication is better in my opinion.' He then contrasts: 'but with emails it's kind of, you know, it takes a bit for back and forth… it just doesn't feel as personal to me.'
During the phone-call portion (approximately 0–8 s), the interviewee uses broad, open-palm hand gestures, moving both hands outward and upward in rhythm with his speech. His head tilts and nods on emphasized words such as 'definitely,' 'voice,' and 'feeling.' His vocal pitch rises on these keywords and he inserts the filler 'um' near the start of the sentence.
At the transition point around 8–9 s ('but with emails'), his hands draw inward toward his torso, his forward lean decreases, and his gesturing amplitude visibly reduces. His pace slows slightly and he introduces the filler phrase 'you know,' repeating it once more near 12 s. The vocal contour flattens relative to the earlier animated delivery.
In the email-description portion (approximately 9–16 s), the interviewee's right hand makes a small dismissive lateral wave around 13–14 s as he says 'it just doesn't feel as personal.' His facial expression shifts from the earlier engaged, slightly smiling look to a more neutral, matter-of-fact appearance. His hands rest lower on the desk surface toward the end of the clip.
The interviewee's speech contains repeated structural phrases: 'just communication is better in my opinion' and 'it just doesn't feel as personal to me,' bookending the two modalities he contrasts. Fillers 'um' and 'you know' appear in both halves but cluster more densely in the email half (two instances of 'you know' within roughly four seconds).

At approximately 0–1 s, the examiner (an older man with short dark hair, glasses, and a light grey button-up shirt, seated across the desk holding papers) turns his head toward the interviewee and asks, 'And why is that?' in a brief, level-toned prompt. His mouth moves minimally and his posture remains seated and forward-facing.
Beginning around 1 s, the interviewee (young man with curly brown hair, grey crew-neck sweatshirt, seated at the desk with stacked papers and a dark filing cabinet behind him) responds: 'I I really think it's just because you can't see their face, um, it's definitely just not the same. I think I'd probably say.' The doubled 'I' occurs at the very onset of his utterance before he continues into the full sentence.
During the interviewee's response (roughly 1–8 s), his hands remain resting on the desk surface with only slight, low-amplitude finger movements; no broad open-palm gestures or outward arm sweeps are visible, in contrast to the wider gesturing noted in the earlier phone-call segment.
The interviewee's gaze shifts slightly downward and to his left during the middle of his answer (around 3–5 s, on 'you can't see their face'), then returns toward the examiner's direction as he finishes with 'I think I'd probably say.' His head tilts marginally forward rather than nodding emphatically.
The filler 'um' appears mid-sentence after 'their face' (approximately 4 s), delivered with a brief pause and a slight drop in pitch before he resumes at 'it's definitely just not the same.'
The interviewee's final phrase, 'I think I'd probably say,' trails off without completing a comparative statement; his mouth closes and his expression settles into a neutral, slightly downturned look as the clip ends around 8–9 s.
Vocal delivery across the response is slower and flatter in pitch contour compared to the earlier animated segment described in prior observations; syllable rate is reduced, and the overall volume appears even without sharp rises on keywords.
The on-screen subtitle text reads: 'just doesn't feel as personal to me. Why is that? I really think it's just because you can't see their face um it's definitely just not the same I think I'd probably say.' confirming the spoken content and the examiner's preceding question.

The interviewee opens with a quick confirmation repetition ('Yeah, yes definitely'), followed by a filler 'Um, first off,' before launching into a concrete scenario about being on a train in public. The initial hesitation marker does not recur after the 'Um'; the remainder of the 10-second window flows as a single descriptive sentence without further pauses or restarts.
Visually, the interviewee sits at a desk in an office-like room (stacked papers, filing cabinet behind him), wearing a grey sweatshirt. For the first four seconds his hands rest together on the desk surface while he delivers the confirmation and filler. From roughly 5 seconds onward, his right hand lifts and extends outward, palm-down, gesturing across the papers on the desk as he says 'I'm in public, I'm on the train,' physically mapping the spatial framing of the scenario onto the tabletop in front of him.
The self-report content is limited to describing a third-party action: hearing someone else on their phone talking while the interviewee is on a train. No personal emotional evaluation is voiced within this window; the statement remains descriptive of the public-space setting and the other person's behavior.
Vocal delivery across the window is steady in volume and pace after the opening 'Um.' The interviewee's gaze shifts slightly to his left (toward the desk/papers) during the hand gesture, then returns forward, consistent with illustrating a scene rather than reading from notes.

In the 0–12 s window the interviewee delivers a firm evaluative statement—'It's the most annoying thing ever'—at roughly 2–4 s with steady forward gaze and hands resting on the desk. Immediately after, at approximately 4–5 s, he repeats 'I'll I'll tell you that'; the visual frames at 4–6 s show him breaking into a broad smile/laugh while looking forward toward the examiner, indicating the repetition is accompanied by self-amusement rather than a visible search for words.
From 6–9 s he continues, 'You know you hear their whole conversation. You know what I mean?' His right hand lifts and gestures loosely outward above the desk (frames 7–9 s), palms open, as if illustrating the spread of sound. His gaze remains generally forward during the gesture.
At 9–10 s he begins 'It's…' then trails into 'I don't know' (10–12 s). Frames 10–11 s show his hands lowering back toward the desk surface and his head tilting slightly downward; the brow area appears relaxed rather than furrowed in the available frames. The vocal delivery of 'I don't know' is softer and lower in energy than the preceding complaint, functioning as a conversational tag rather than a full stop.
At 12 s the shot cuts to the examiner—a man in a grey button-down shirt and glasses, holding a stack of papers—seated across the desk, looking toward the interviewee. This cut marks a turn-taking boundary; no further speech from the interviewee is captured within this clip.
Taken together within this window, the 'I'll I'll' stumble coincides with a smile (suggesting rhetorical softening of an emphatic point) and the trailing 'I don't know' coincides with lowered hands and a slight downward gaze shift (suggesting the complaint is being wound down rather than abandoned mid-thought). The gaze does not drift far downward; it stays largely forward until the final two seconds.

The interviewer (older man, glasses, light shirt) poses the question 'Do you enjoy traveling to different places?' in a calm, measured tone while holding papers (0–3 s).
The interviewee (young man, curly hair, grey sweatshirt) responds immediately without hesitation: 'Oh absolutely, I love traveling to new countries' (3–6 s), delivered at a noticeably faster pace than the question.
He then constructs a specific claim: 'If you probably took a map out right now of the UK, I've probably visited almost every place here' (6–9 s), naming the country and using the superlative 'almost every place.'
Continuing, he says 'You could point out a spot, I've probably been there um' (9–12 s); around 11 s he leans forward and brings both hands together in front of his torso, a gesture that loosely tracks the verbal image of indicating a location on a map, though it reads as a general emphatic motion rather than a precise pointing action.
The utterance trails off with the filler 'um' at approximately 12 s, suggesting the thought is incomplete or he is searching for a next example.
Overall delivery is fluent and rapid with minimal pausing until the final filler; the content moves from a general enthusiasm statement to a concrete geographic claim within roughly nine seconds.

The interviewee (young man, curly hair, grey sweatshirt, seated at a desk with papers and a filing cabinet behind him) finishes his prior geographic claim with 'probably been there' followed by the filler 'um' at approximately 0–1 s, his gaze directed slightly downward toward the desk.
From roughly 1–6 s, he delivers the constraint explanation: 'the only reason I don't travel as much as I would like is just because I don't have as much time and money, you know, as I feel like I would need to do that.' His speaking pace is noticeably slower than his earlier rapid delivery; he inserts the fillers 'um' (at the start) and 'you know' (mid-sentence). His hands rest near the desk surface with small, low-amplitude movements; his facial expression remains largely neutral, mouth moving steadily, eyes shifting between the desk and a forward point.
At approximately 6–7 s he utters another 'Um' as a brief pause, then pivots: 'but I love it. I get to meet new people, see new faces, things like that.' His tone lifts in energy and pace returns to a quicker rhythm. Visually, around 7–10 s his eyebrows raise slightly and his mouth opens wider on 'love it'; he gestures with both hands in a small outward motion while listing 'new people, see new faces.'
Around 10–11 s, while still finishing 'things like that, you know,' he extends his right hand toward a stack of papers on the desk and picks one up, holding it loosely. His posture leans slightly forward.
At approximately 11–13 s the interviewer's voice enters off-screen with 'So tell me what places have you been in the UK?' The interviewee, still holding the paper, turns his head slightly toward the interviewer's direction and nods faintly, his expression shifting to an attentive, mildly smiling look as he prepares to respond.
Throughout the 0–13 s window the camera remains a fixed medium shot; no cuts or zooms occur. The IELTS tester watermark and 'IELTS SPEAKING TEST' badge are visible in the lower-right corner.

At approximately 0–1 s the interviewee (young man, curly brown hair, grey sweatshirt, seated at a dark desk with a filing cabinet and stacked papers behind him) produces a prolonged 'Uh' as an audible onset before speaking. His gaze is directed slightly to his right toward the interviewer's off-screen position; both hands rest near the desk surface with index fingers lightly touching. The 'Uh' is not followed by a restart or silent search pause—he immediately launches into a complete clause, indicating it functions as a discourse marker rather than a word-retrieval hesitation.
From roughly 1–7 s he enumerates 'I've been to London, Birmingham, Manchester with my friends during the holidays' in a flat, list-like cadence with even pacing and minimal pitch variation. His hands maintain the finger-touching gesture, making small rhythmic taps as each city name is spoken. Eye direction stays predominantly toward the interviewer's side with one brief downward glance to the desk around 4–5 s. Facial expression remains neutral; mouth moves steadily without widening.
At approximately 7–8 s a second 'uh' introduces the next segment: 'London Bridge is probably my favorite.' The speaking pace visibly slows and the intonation contour becomes more varied, with a slight rise on 'favorite.' Simultaneously his hand configuration changes: the touching index fingers separate and both hands draw together into a loosely clasped position at mid-torso level. His gaze shifts marginally more forward (away from the interviewer's side) for about one second before returning.
From 10–13 s he continues 'and then probably next would be the Prehistoric Museum.' Both hands open outward from the clasp into a small, symmetrical explanatory gesture (palms facing each other, moving apart by a few centimetres). His eyebrows lift slightly and his mouth opens wider on 'Prehistoric,' giving the delivery a warmer, more engaged quality compared with the earlier flat list. Gaze returns to the interviewer's direction. The camera remains a fixed medium shot throughout; the ieltstester.com watermark and IELTS Speaking Test badge stay in the lower-right corner.

[0.0–2.0 s, audio_video] Justin (interviewee, curly brown hair, grey sweatshirt) completes the clause 'and after that probably the art galleries around there' with a slight upward inflection on 'there.' Both hands are open, palms facing inward, making a small enclosing gesture at chest height before settling onto the desk surface.
[2.0–4.0 s, video] Justin's hands come together, fingers interlaced, resting on the dark desk. His gaze remains directed slightly to his right (toward the examiner's off-screen position). His mouth closes; he listens. Facial expression is neutral, eyebrows relaxed.
[3.5–4.5 s, audio] The examiner (off-screen at this point) says 'Hmm, excellent' in a low, approving tone. No visual of the examiner yet.
[4.5–5.0 s, video] Camera cuts to the examiner: middle-aged man, short dark hair, glasses, light blue-grey button-down shirt, seated across the same desk. He holds a small stack of white papers in both hands.
[5.0–9.0 s, audio_video] The examiner looks down at his papers, flips or adjusts a page with his right thumb, and delivers the transition: 'Now… moving on to talking about your hometown in France.' The word 'Now' is drawn out with a slight pause before the rest of the sentence. His gaze stays on the papers for most of the utterance, lifting briefly toward Justin near the end. Justin is off-screen during this segment.
[9.0–10.0 s, video] The examiner finishes the sentence, glances up from the papers toward Justin's direction, and holds the papers steady. His expression is attentive, awaiting response.

The interviewee (young man with curly hair in a grey sweatshirt) opens his answer with an emphatic, confident affirmation for children: 'Oh yeah, children absolutely,' delivered with hands clasped together on the desk and a slight forward lean toward the interviewer.
When he transitions to discussing teenagers around the 7-second mark, his vocal pace noticeably slows and becomes more hedging ('I'd probably say not so much'), and his hand activity shifts from clasped stillness to fingers tapping and moving across the desk surface.
He structures the contrast between age groups by first providing concrete positive reasons for children (open fields and parks to play in), then listing specific missing facilities for teenagers (movie theaters, gyms, cafes), creating a parallel but oppositional framework.
During the teenager portion, his eye direction drops intermittently toward the desk as he searches for examples of facilities, then returns toward the interviewer when he circles back to reaffirm children ('but definitely children, yes younger children').
The interviewer (older man with glasses holding papers) prompts with 'And why?' at the start and follows up with a new question about hometown changes at approximately 19 seconds, framing the interviewee's two-part response within a single exchange.

At the start of the clip (approximately 0–2 s), the interviewee—a young man with curly brown hair in a grey sweatshirt, seated at a dark desk with hands clasped—produces a drawn-out 'Hmm' vocalization while his gaze drifts slightly upward and to his left, away from the examiner visible in the opening frame.
From roughly 2 s onward he begins speaking continuously: 'it's an interesting question, yeah, Dunkirk is a very historic town, especially after World War Two.' His posture remains forward-leaning with forearms on the desk; minimal hand movement is visible during this framing statement.
Between approximately 8 s and 13 s he continues: 'just because a lot of the town was left in ruins after the war, and you can still see now to this day…' During this stretch his hands separate briefly into a small open-palm gesture around 10 s, then return to a clasped position. Head nods are subtle and infrequent.
From roughly 14 s to 19 s he enumerates specific remnants: 'old churches and shipwrecks and things like that, which are still standing, uh to—' His pace remains steady; the filler 'uh' appears near the end of the clip as the sentence trails off.
